notes.audience: Các lập trình viên, kỹ sư DevOps và dân tự host server tại Việt Nam đang tìm kiếm giải pháp CLI coding agent chạy trên Linux VPS hoặc GPU nội bộ với chi phí rẻ thay cho Claude Code và Aider.
notes.angle: Thay vì trả phí API đắt đỏ cho Claude Code hay cấu hình Aider phức tạp, Memdoor dùng Team Mode phối hợp 5 model mã nguồn mở giá rẻ (như Qwen 27B) trên Linux để đạt kết quả giải code ngang ngửa frontier model với giá chưa tới 10.000 VNĐ một bài toán.

facts.fact: Memdoor là CLI coding agent được viết hoàn toàn bằng Go dưới giấy phép mã nguồn mở Apache-2.0 và gói gọn trong một file binary duy nhất.
facts.quote: The CLI coding agent in one Go binary. Press Shift+Tab and Go Team Mode.

facts.fact: Quy trình Team Mode gồm 5 agent Qwen3.8-27B đạt điểm trung bình 9.8/10 trên 10 bài toán LiveCodeBench Hard, vượt qua mức 8.0 của Fable 5 chạy đơn lẻ.
facts.quote: Five Qwen3.8-27B agents beat Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard, as a Memdoor workflow.

facts.fact: Chi phí giải một bài toán lập trình khó qua OpenRouter chỉ tốn trung vị 0.39 USD trong 40 phút (tổng 35.79 USD cho toàn bộ 50 lượt chạy).
facts.quote: Cost: a median of 40 minutes and $0.39 a run; $35.79 for the 50.

facts.fact: Kiến trúc Team Mode (dựa trên nghiên cứu GVS5H) chia việc cho 5 vai trò: planner, 2 ideator chạy song song, solver, manager/review và repair worker.
facts.quote: a planner, two ideators, a solver, a manager and a repair worker, each from a fresh context, talking only through files on disk

facts.fact: Theo bài báo GVS5H, phương pháp điều phối không cần huấn luyện giúp Qwen3.8-27B tự host tăng độ chính xác từ 66.8% lên 92.4% pass@1 trên LiveCodeBench.
facts.quote: locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%.

facts.fact: Mỗi agent trong team chạy trên một context mới hoàn toàn (fresh context) và trao đổi thông tin độc quyền qua các file trên ổ cứng thay vì nhồi chat history.
facts.quote: Every agent prompt: "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat"; the paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain.

facts.fact: Model phán đoán Jev (TypeSafe) phản hồi dưới 0.5 giây giúp cắt giảm token đầu vào khi tra cứu codebase từ 54,661 xuống 14,367 tokens (−74%).
facts.quote: a codebase question 54,661 to 14,367 input tokens (−74%); an edit with a test and ten one-file fixes read the same files either way (within ±11%)

facts.fact: Cấu hình phần cứng tối thiểu để tự chạy team-solve offline là model 27B lượng hóa Q5 trở lên trên GPU 24 GB VRAM hoặc máy Mac 32 GB RAM.
facts.quote: Floor for team-solve: a 27B at Q5 or above, a 24 GB card or a 32 GB Mac.

facts.fact: Chạy giải một bài toán khó trên card 24 GB ngốn khoảng 300,000 output tokens qua 8 bước và mất khoảng 4 giờ với tốc độ sinh 20 tokens/giây.
facts.quote: Cost of a hard problem: about 300K output tokens over eight steps, about four hours at 20 tokens a second on a 24 GB card.

facts.fact: Memdoor khuyến nghị dùng runtime janis chạy trên port 8090 để chạy model và phục vụ cả decision model cục bộ không cần API key.
facts.quote: janis is the runtime we recommend: one Go server, open models on a Mac's GPU through MLX or on an NVIDIA box through CUDA, on port 8090.

facts.fact: Mặc định Ollama chỉ nhận 4,096 tokens ngữ cảnh, không đủ cho prompt lập trình nên bắt buộc phải thiết lập OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768.
facts.quote: Ollama reads 4,096 tokens of prompt unless told otherwise. A coder turn's prompt is longer; the model then answers a task it never saw and calls no tool.

facts.fact: Tính năng /remote cung cấp đường link mã hóa đầu-cuối và mã QR để mở giao diện dòng lệnh trực tiếp trên điện thoại.
facts.quote: This conversation on your phone: a link and a QR code, the terminal itself, end-to-end encrypted

caveats: Context window mặc định của Ollama là 4,096 tokens, khiến model trả lời sai hoặc không gọi tool; bắt buộc phải set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 hoặc tạo Modelfile riêng.
Prompt của quy trình team-solve tích hợp sẵn trong CLI khác với bộ prompt gốc của nhóm tác giả nghiên cứu GVS5H, do đó điểm số 9.8/10 không phản ánh trực tiếp bản built-in.
Tài khoản không nạp tiền dùng model miễn phí (:free) trên OpenRouter sẽ bị thu thập dữ liệu huấn luyện (mang cờ allow).
Rủi ro phản xạ sai: Trong benchmark, manager từng tự bịa test phản ví dụ sai khiến cả team viết lại làm hỏng một chương trình vốn đã đúng.

Yêu cầu phần cứng tự host tại chỗ khá nặng: model 7B/8B nhanh bị mất mạch suy luận; team-solve yêu cầu tối thiểu model 27B Q5 trở lên, ngốn ~300K output tokens và mất khoảng 4 giờ xử lý trên card 24 GB VRAM.
gaps: Khả năng xử lý yêu cầu và tài liệu codebase bằng tiếng Việt của các model mã nguồn mở nhỏ (như Qwen 27B) trong Team Mode có mượt không?
Cấu hình tối thiểu về CPU/RAM của VPS Linux là bao nhiêu nếu chỉ chạy Memdoor làm Gateway kết nối OpenRouter API (không chạy model local)?
Có cơ chế giới hạn ngân sách (budget cap) trực tiếp trên CLI để tránh trường hợp vòng lặp workflow tiêu lẹm quá số tiền API mong muốn hay không?
Việc tùy chỉnh vai trò thành viên trong Team Mode (thay thế ideator bằng linter/security auditor) có thể làm nhanh qua file config hay bắt buộc phải tự viết lại toàn bộ YAML workflow?

## guregodevo/memdoor (https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor)
Description: The CLI coding agent with Team Mode: cheap models, frontier results.
Homepage: https://memdoor.ai
Language: Go; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-10-05; last push 2026-11-10
Latest release: v1.814.0 (2026-11-09)
README (start):
Memdoor
  Team Mode: cheap models, frontier results.The CLI coding agent in one Go binary. Press Shift+Tab and Go Team Mode. Five Qwen3.8-27B agents beat Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard, every run published. Ollama, llama.cpp, or any key. No account.
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
  

> **Five Qwen3.8-27B agents beat Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard, as a Memdoor workflow.**
> [GVS5H](https://github.com/slee-persis/GVS5H)'s harness rebuilt with the
> authors' exact prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their list, five
> passes each: a mean of **9.8 of 10**. The authors' own harness scored 9.6 and
> Fable 5 in a single call 8.0, the gap the authors measured on these ten
> (across their full 100: 92.4 and 90.4). All 50 runs are published: every
> request, reply, program and grader output. The workflow is YAML and names no
> model. Point it at yours, or at a local one with `memdoor connect local`
> (janis, the runtime we recommend; Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM and LM Studio
> work too; [how to run it on an open-weight model,
> no key](https://memdoor.ai/docs/open-weight)).
> [examples/workflows/team-solve](examples/workflows/team-solve/) · [the result page](https://memdoor.ai/docs/team-solve) · [the HN thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50320995)

Memdoor is a coding agent and workflow runner. Give the agent a task to read
files, edit code and run checks. For repeatable work, a workflow coordinates
checked steps, parallel tasks and approval gates. Run it with a local model or
a provider on your key.

On this machine:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...    # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, …
# or no key: memdoor connect local    # janis and an open-weight model on this machine — https://memdoor.ai/docs/open-weight
cd your-project && memdoor             # the first run sets the machine up
memdoor workflow try                   # two minutes: the team on a sample problem, ending in a verdict
memdoor cron add --workflow team-backlog "0 2 * * *"   # one open issue a night, a pull request when its Check passed
```

The install or the first run did not finish: [open an Install issue](https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/issues/new?template=install.md).

On a box reachable by ssh, nothing installed there:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash          # here, once
memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box                           # installs memdoor on the box, starts its gateway, opens the window on it
memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box connect openrouter        # your key, kept on the box; every turn there runs on it
memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box run "fix the failing test" # the same box from a script or CI
```

**Decision model.** Jev (TypeSafe) answers a typed question about a turn
with a calibrated probability in under half a second. Judged reads: search,
file and log reads return what counts. Per-turn toolbox: only the tools the
turn needs are sent. Stall detection: a turn that stops making progress ends.
44 paired runs, decisions off and on: 22 of 22 passed each way; a codebase
question 54,661 to 14,367 input tokens (−74%); an edit with a test and ten
one-file fixes read the same files either way (within ±11%)
([`docs/features/DECIDE.md`](docs/features/DECIDE.md)).

**Workflows, the deterministic harness.** Say the steps; the coder writes one
YAML per step. [`mario`](https://github.com/guregodevo/mario) runs the graph.
Independent steps run in parallel. A step is done when its check passes. A
gate waits for approval with the diff. A failed run resumes at the failed
step. Started by hand, from CI or on local cron
([`docs/features/WORKFLOWS.md`](docs/features/WORKFLOWS.md)). Workflows, not
skills: [the write-up](https://guregodevo.github.io/2026/10/06/workflows-not-skills/).
Examples, each run before it was added:
[`examples/workflows/`](examples/workflows/). The nightly grade step,
`examples/workflows/nightly-rule/steps/grade.yaml`:

```yaml
type: agent
prompt: |
  Today's partition is {{.partition}}.
  Read rules/{{.partition}}.md and grade today's trading rule: assess it
  briefly (clarity, risk profile, plausibility) and write a JSON object
  {"score": <0-100 integer>, "verdict": ""} into
  grades/{{.partition}}.json (create grades/ if needed).
requires:
  - table_pattern: build
target:
  # run by the engine, not by the agent: the grade must exist and be newer than step 1's start stamp
  command: test "grades/{{.partition}}.json" -nt "rules/{{.partition}}.start" && test -s "grades/{{.partition}}.json"
timeout: 10m
```

The review loop recorded (findings verified by running, a gate, the fixes
applied): [memdoor.ai/workflows](https://memdoor.ai/workflows).

## In the window

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/model` | The agent's ladder, cheapest rung first. Pin any model of your providers. List prices |
| `/connect` | Add a provider: OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Baseten, Groq, xAI, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a company AI gateway. `/connect local`: janis on this machine or the box, or Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM; no key. `/connect chatgpt`: a ChatGPT Plus/Pro plan, no key |
| `/w` | The project's workflows and runs. `/w  [the task]` runs one (`/w team-solve `), enter opens a run's graph, `a` approves a gate |
| `/usage` | This month on your key, per model, and what the decision model kept out of the bill |
| `/remote` | This conversation on your phone: a link and a QR code, the terminal itself, end-to-end encrypted |
| `/remote view` | A watch-only link: live, no typing, no account, up to 200 viewers. `?live=1` is the terminal alone, for a stream or OBS |
| `/files` or `ctrl+f` | The project's files, the ones this conversation read or changed first, each with what happened to it. Enter previews, `ctrl+d` diffs, `ctrl+e` opens in `$EDITOR`, tab puts `@path` in the prompt |
| `/graph` or `ctrl+g` | The turn as a graph: the reads, the edits that depended on them, the runs that depended on the edits, the failing check in red |
| `/mcp` | MCP servers from a URL, a command or a `.mcp.json` snippet |
| `/help` | The rest |

`Esc` interrupts. `ctrl+o` expands tool frames. `Shift+Tab` switches the mode,
auto or team. `ctrl+t` sets the reasoning effort. `@path` mentions a file. `MEMDOOR_APPROVE=changes` asks before every
command and write.

## In your editor

`memdoor acp` serves the coder over the [Agent Client
Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com). Zed and JetBrains host it
natively. VS Code: an ACP client extension (for example "ACP Client") and one
setting:

```json
"acp.agents": { "Memdoor": { "command": "memdoor", "args": ["acp"] } }
```

A session is a conversation on the local gateway. A prompt is a turn in the
editor's workspace folder. Text, tool calls and approvals show as the
editor's own. Steps: [memdoor.ai/docs/editor](https://memdoor.ai/docs/editor).

## From a script

```bash
memdoor run "make the retry wait configurable and add a test"     # a headless turn, no window
git diff | memdoor run "review this diff; one line per finding"    # stdin is the input
memdoor run --json "fix the failing test" | jq 'select(.event=="done")'
memdoor workflow run release --wait                                 # progress on stderr, results on stdout
memdoor remote --last                                               # the link /remote gives, on stdout; the gateway holds the run for your phone
memdoor remote --view --last                                        # the watch-only link: an audience, or a pair of eyes
```

Exit code: 0 checked, 2 unverified or a failing check, 3 a question nobody
answered (`--yes` answers it), 1 an error, 130 interrupted. The gateway starts
if none is running. `memdoor resume` opens any run.
[Headless, then attached](https://memdoor.ai/docs/headless).

## In GitHub Actions

One step. Your key as the secret. Nothing added to the repo
([Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/memdoor)):

```yaml
on: pull_request
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: guregodevo/memdoor-action@v1
        with:
          workflow: pr-review
          openrouter-api-key: ${{ secrets.OPEN_ROUTER_API_KEY }}
```

Built in:

- **`pr-triage`**: ready for review, needs work, or likely slop, from checks run in the job (the tests, claimed tests that are not there, functions nothing calls).
- **`pr-review`**: findings verified by running the code; the job fails only on a blocker.
- **`security-review`**: secrets, injection, path traversal, missing authorization.
- **`write-tests`**: tests for what the change touches; the job fails when one shows the change is wrong.
- **`pr-description`**: title, What, Why, How to test, Risk.
- **`explain-failure`**: a failed run's logs and the diff; the cause, file:line, the fix.
- **`issue-triage`**: labels, kind, summary, duplicates.
- **`fix-tests`**: finds the test command, fixes the code until the tests pass, leaves the fix in the working tree.
- **`release-notes`**: commits since the last tag as Added / Changed / Fixed.
- **`team-solve`**: the task a prompt defines (`memdoor workflow run team-solve ""`), done by a team of fresh contexts, GVS5H's method on any task and any model: changes across a repository checked by its own tests, a program by its samples, a document by a fresh judge. Its prompts differ from the published steps', so the 9.8 above is theirs, not the built-in's.
- **`team-backlog`**: the repository's open issues, unattended: the next issue nobody is on, team-solve on it in a branch, a pull request when the Check passed, a comment on the issue when it did not; one issue a run, on a cron (`memdoor cron add --workflow team-backlog "0 2 * * *"`).

`local-model: Qwen3-8B-4bit` in place of the key: the model runs inside the
runner ([janis](https://github.com/guregodevo/janis), one file, cached), one
call. On a free runner: an obvious and a subtle bug found in about a minute
each; a correct change can be flagged as a blocker. A first pass.

`workflow: ` runs yours from `.memdoor/workflows//`. Exit code:
0 done, 2 failed, 1 stopped, 3 stopped at an approval gate. The job summary
holds the review, the fix or the notes. Trigger on `pull_request`, never
`pull_request_target`: a fork's pull request gets no secrets.

## Keys and models

A provider key in the environment (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`,
`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, …) or `memdoor connect`. No key: the
first `memdoor` signs in with OpenRouter in the browser, from this machine,
over ssh or on a box. No credit: a free model, 50 requests a day; its hosts
train on what they are sent. For a trial, not private code.

Local: `memdoor connect local` installs [janis](https://github.com/guregodevo/janis),
the runtime we recommend, or connects a running Ollama, llama.cpp or LM Studio.
Nothing leaves it. janis: one Go server, open models on a Mac's GPU through
MLX or an NVIDIA box through CUDA, serves chat and the decision model, no
key; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B on a $0.71-an-hour Google L4. On a box: `memdoor
--gateway ssh://you@box connect local`. Peers: `memdoor peers add box
http://box:18789 --dir ~/app` names the box; `@box:coder …` in any
conversation runs the turn there and returns the answer.

## Where your data goes

Files, sessions and commands stay on your machine. What the model reads goes
to the provider. OpenRouter: every request carries `data_collection: deny`;
hosts that train on paid inputs are kept out of the ladders. Exception: a
`:free` model, pinned or answering for an account with no credit; its hosts
train on what they are sent, the request says so (`allow`), Memdoor warns at
the pin or at connect. Vendor key or company gateway: nothing else is
contacted. [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md) lists the hosts the binary
can name; a test fails the build on a new one.

# Claude Code

[npm]: https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@anthropic-ai/claude-code.svg?style=flat-square

Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal, understands your codebase, and helps you code faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows -- all through natural language commands. Use it in your terminal, IDE, or tag @claude on Github.

**Learn more in the [official documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview)**.

## Get started
> [!NOTE]
> Installation via npm is deprecated. Use one of the recommended methods below.

For more installation options, uninstall steps, and troubleshooting, see the [setup documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup).

1. Install Claude Code:

    **MacOS/Linux (Recommended):**
    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
    ```

    **Homebrew (MacOS/Linux):**
    ```bash
    brew install --cask claude-code
    ```

    **Windows (Recommended):**
    ```powershell
    irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
    ```

    **WinGet (Windows):**
    ```powershell
    winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode
    ```

    **NPM (Deprecated):**
    ```bash
    npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
    ```

2. Navigate to your project directory and run `claude`.

## Plugins

Anthropic's Claude Code plugins are developed in [claude-plugins-official](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official). See the [plugins directory](./plugins/README.md) for more about plugins.

## Reporting Bugs

We welcome your feedback. Use the `/bug` command to report issues directly within Claude Code, or file a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues).

## Connect on Discord

Join the [Claude Developers Discord](https://anthropic.com/discord) to connect with other developers using Claude Code. Get help, share feedback, and discuss your projects with the community.

## Data collection, usage, and retention

When you use Claude Code, we collect feedback, which includes usage data (such as code acceptance or rejections), associated conversation data, and user feedback submitted via the `/bug` command.

### How we use your data

See our [data usage policies](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage).

### Privacy safeguards

We have implemented several safeguards to protect your data, including limited retention periods for sensitive information, restricted access to user session data, and clear policies against using feedback for model training.

For full details, please review our [Commercial Terms of Service](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms) and [Privacy Policy](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/privacy).

## herdrdev/herdr (https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr)
Description: the runtime your coding agents live on
Homepage: https://herdr.dev
Language: Rust; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-03-27; last push 2026-11-07
Latest release: v0.9.5 (2026-10-14)
README (start):
# herdr

  

  herdr.dev · install · quick start · docs

  English · 简体中文

  
  
  
  
  
  

---

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/043ec09f-4bdd-41d5-aee0-8fda6b83e267

**the runtime your coding agents live on.**

- **detach without stopping work** — herdr keeps terminals running in a background server when you close the client or lose your SSH connection. after a server or machine restart, herdr restores the saved layout and can resume supported agent sessions; the original processes do not survive. [session state →](https://herdr.dev/docs/session-state/)
- **several machines, one window** — keep local work and saved ssh machines together, with a combined agent list and independent reconnects. [remote machines →](https://herdr.dev/docs/connecting-machines/)
- **never hunt for the stuck one** — every pane is marked working, blocked, or idle. when an agent stops and needs an answer, herdr says so.
- **agent-native** — agents drive herdr through the cli and socket api: they can spawn panes, prompt each other, and wait until another agent is genuinely blocked. [agent skill →](https://herdr.dev/docs/agent-skill/)
- **runs what you already run** — claude code, codex, cursor, opencode, grok and the rest. herdr doesn't wrap or replace them; it owns their terminals. building an agent? [add herdr support →](https://herdr.dev/docs/add-herdr-support/)
- **keyboard and mouse, both first-class** — tmux-style prefix keys *and* click, drag, split. pick per moment, not per tool.
- **plugins** — extend panes and workflows. [browse the marketplace →](https://herdr.dev/plugins/)
- **one rust binary, no electron** — runs in whatever terminal you already use.

---

## install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh
```

or `brew install herdr` · `mise use -g herdr` · windows: `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://herdr.dev/install.ps1 | iex"` · [endpoint-protected Windows](https://herdr.dev/docs/windows-beta/) · [binaries](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/releases)

then start it where the work lives:

```bash
herdr
```

README (start):
AI Pair Programming in Your Terminal

Aider lets you pair program with LLMs to start a new project or build on your existing codebase. 

  

  
  
  
  
  
  

## Features

### [Cloud and local LLMs](https://aider.chat/docs/llms.html)

Aider works best with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1 & Chat V3, OpenAI o1, o3-mini & GPT-4o, but can connect to almost any LLM, including local models.

### [Maps your codebase](https://aider.chat/docs/repomap.html)

Aider makes a map of your entire codebase, which helps it work well in larger projects.

### [100+ code languages](https://aider.chat/docs/languages.html)

Aider works with most popular programming languages: python, javascript, rust, ruby, go, cpp, php, html, css, and dozens more.

### [Git integration](https://aider.chat/docs/git.html)

Aider automatically commits changes with sensible commit messages. Use familiar git tools to easily diff, manage and undo AI changes.

### [Use in your IDE](https://aider.chat/docs/usage/watch.html)

Use aider from within your favorite IDE or editor. Ask for changes by adding comments to your code and aider will get to work.

### [Images & web pages](https://aider.chat/docs/usage/images-urls.html)

Add images and web pages to the chat to provide visual context, screenshots, reference docs, etc.

### [Voice-to-code](https://aider.chat/docs/usage/voice.html)

Speak with aider about your code! Request new features, test cases or bug fixes using your voice and let aider implement the changes.

### [Linting & testing](https://aider.chat/docs/usage/lint-test.html)

Automatically lint and test your code every time aider makes changes. Aider can fix problems detected by your linters and test suites.

### [Copy/paste to web chat](https://aider.chat/docs/usage/copypaste.html)

Work with any LLM via its web chat interface. Aider streamlines copy/pasting code context and edits back and forth with a browser.

## Getting Started

```bash
python -m pip install aider-install
aider-install

# Change directory into your codebase
cd /to/your/project

# DeepSeek
aider --model deepseek --api-key deepseek=

# Claude 3.7 Sonnet
aider --model sonnet --api-key anthropic=

# o3-mini
aider --model o3-mini --api-key openai=
```

See the [installation instructions](https://aider.chat/docs/install.html) and [usage documentation](https://aider.chat/docs/usage.html) for more details.

## restlessronin/llm-code-highlighter (https://github.com/restlessronin/llm-code-highlighter)
Description: Condense source code for LLM analysis by extracting essential highlights, utilizing a simplified version of Paul Gauthier's repomap technique from Aider Chat.
Homepage: https://www.npmjs.com/package/llm-code-highlighter
Language: TypeScript; license: Apache-2.0; created 2023-12-21; last push 2024-03-03
No releases
README (start):
# llm-code-highlighter

**llm-code-highlighter** is a TypeScript library for creating succinct repository highlights, based on a simplified version of Paul Gauthier's repomap technique as outlined in the [Aider Chat docs](https://aider.chat/docs/repomap.html) and implemented by the code in the [aider](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider) and [grep-ast](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/grep-ast) repos.

This typescript version of the original python code was created with assistance from ChatGPT 4. Every line of code was manually curated (by me, @restlessronin 😇).

## Installation

At the moment, this plugin is only being actively developed against the [Continue repository](https://github.com/continuedev/continue). If you are interested in other use cases, please [file an issue on the repository](https://github.com/restlessronin/llm-code-highlighter/issues) and I'll see what I can do to accommodate.

To install llm-code-highlighter, you can use npm or yarn:

```bash
npm install llm-code-highlighter
```

### Usage

To use llm-code-highlighter in your TypeScript project, you need to import the required functions:

```typescript
import { getHighlightsThatFit, getOutlines, ILLMContextSizer } from 'llm-code-highlighter';
```

`getHighlightsThatFit`

This function identifies highlights within the code by selecting high-ranked tags from "chat" and "other" source files. It then determines and returns the maximum number of highlighted lines, exclusively from "other" sources, that can be included within the token budget defined by the ContextSizer.

```typescript
const contextSizer = {
  fits(content: string): boolean {
    return content.length <= 100;
  },
} as ILLMContextSizer;

const chatSources = [
  {
    relPath: 'chat1.js',
    code: `
          console.log(add(1, 2));
        `,
  },
  {
    relPath: 'chat2.js',
    code: `
          console.log(multiply(3, 1));
        `,
  },
];

const otherSources = [
  {
    relPath: 'file1.js',
    code: `
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
console.log(add(1, 2));
`,
  },
  {
    relPath: 'file2.js',
    code: `
function subtract(a, b) {
  return a - b;
}
console.log(subtract(3, 1));
`,
  },
  {
    relPath: 'file3.js',
    code: `
function multiply(a, b) {
  return a * b;
}
console.log(multiply(2, 3));
`,
  },
];

const result = await getHighlightsThatFit(contextSizer, chatSources, otherSources);
console.log(result);
// Output:
// file1.js
// ⋮...
// █function add(a, b) {
// ⋮...
//
// file3.js
// ⋮...
// █function multiply(a, b) {
// ⋮...
```

`getOutlines`

This function generates an outline for a set of files by only displaying the definition lines. It takes an array of objects, each containing the path and source code for a file. The function generates outlines for each of the files, concatenates all of them, and returns the result as a single string.

```typescript
const sources = [
  {
    relPath: 'file1.js',
    code: `
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}`,
  },
  {
    relPath: 'file2.js',
    code: `
function subtract(a, b) {
  return a - b;
}`,
  },
];

const outlines = await getOutlines(sources);

console.log(outlines);
// Output:
// file1.js
// █function add(a, b) {
// ⋮...
//
// file2.js
//  █function subtract(a, b) {
// ⋮...
```

Please refer to the source code for more details and options.

## Run Memdoor on an open-weight model, no key — Memdoor docs
URL: https://memdoor.ai/docs/open-weight
Description: A model on your machine is a provider. memdoor connect local finds it, asks for no token. Nothing leaves the box.

Home
Run Memdoor on an open-weight model, no key

A model on your machine is a provider. memdoor connect local finds it, asks for no token. Nothing leaves the box. This page: empty machine to the team-solve workflow on your GPU.

1. Run a model

janis is the runtime we recommend: one Go server, open models on a Mac's GPU through MLX or on an NVIDIA box through CUDA, on port 8090. It also answers the decision model, so the token savings run locally. With nothing running, memdoor connect local (step 3) installs it and the model that fits the machine. By hand:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/guregodevo/janis/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
janis pull                                  # the model that fits this machine
janis serve --detach --model <that model>   # http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1

janis pull with no name picks by RAM: Qwen3.5-9B at 16 GB, Qwen3.8-27B from 32 GB.

Qwen3-8B on a 16 GB M4, one server at a time (the method):

	janis	llama.cpp	Ollama
prefill, 9,000 tokens	195.0 tok/s	174.4 tok/s	154.5 tok/s
decode	22.8 tok/s	19.9 tok/s	20.3 tok/s

janis runs the MLX 4-bit weights (4.3 GB), the other two the Q4_K_M GGUF (5.2 GB).

Any other OpenAI-compatible server serves the chat half; decisions stay off on it. Four common ones:

runtime	start it	listens on
Ollama	ollama pull qwen3:8b	11434
llama.cpp	llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768	8080
LM Studio	load a model, start the server	1234
vLLM	vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B	8000

Model: one trained for tool calls, since a coder turn reads files, calls tools and writes patches. Qwen3.8-27B is the one the published result ran on. A 7B or 8B answers a turn on a laptop but loses the thread on long work. Floor for team-solve: a 27B at Q5 or above, a 24 GB card or a 32 GB Mac.

2. Give it a window

Ollama reads 4,096 tokens of prompt unless told otherwise. A coder turn's prompt is longer; the model then answers a task it never saw and calls no tool. Start Ollama with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 or make a tag:

printf 'FROM qwen3:8b\nPARAMETER num_ctx 32768\n' > Modelfile
ollama create qwen3:8b-32k -f Modelfile

llama.cpp: -c 32768. LM Studio and vLLM: the model's settings. 32K covers a turn. Team-solve replies run past 100K, so give the 27B what the card allows.

3. Connect
curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash
memdoor connect local            # finds the runtime on this machine, probes it, keeps it
memdoor model                    # the model that answers, and what it lists for: nothing

/providers.json

bit                                                                                             
  pinned: new conversations start on local:Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit. /model auto removes the pin.    
  /model <id> in the window pins one of its models; memdoor model search <name> finds them.     
  it judges too: kept as local-decisions, the decision model runs here with no key.             
                                                                                                
→ Next: memdoor --help   (see all commands)                                                     
$ memdoor model                                                                                 
coder      Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit

00:00
memdoor connect local finds janis on this machine, tests Qwen3.5-9B, keeps it and pins it

memdoor connect local lists the model servers on the gateway's machine (janis, Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM, on their default ports). Pick one by number. With none running on Linux or macOS, it offers to install janis and the model that fits the machine. A janis older than the latest release is updated first when it is in ~/.local/bin, where janis's installer puts it. A janis elsewhere is left as is, with the command to update it. On a Mac the check needs a janis that memdoor installed: it keeps the release's checksum in ~/.memdoor/janis-release.sha256. --base http://localhost:8000/v1 names another. The probe reads the model list and makes one call; a large model may take minutes to load. /model search lists what the runtime serves, /model qwen3:8b-32k pins one. A model pulled after the connect is found on its next pin.

In a terminal, connect local keeps the tested model as your pin. New conversations start on local:<model>. /model auto removes the pin.

On a box: memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box connect local installs Memdoor there and connects the box's runtime. @box:coder … here runs the turn on the box (peers).

4. A turn
cd your-project && memdoor tui

Ask it to read a file and fix something small. memdoor meter shows input tokens per call; 4,096 on every call means the window of step 2 is not set.

On janis the first two conversations after a start prefill the whole prompt. Later ones start where the last two parted (janis 0.1.11), and the first answer comes in seconds.

5. The team on your GPU

The team-solve workflow names no model and is built in: it runs the team on whatever connect local found. The 9.8 of 10 on LiveCodeBench Hard is the published steps', with the authors' prompts; the built-in's prompts differ and have no score of their own yet:

mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem
memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait   # built in; an empty folder gets the sample problem

Cost of a hard problem: about 300K output tokens over eight steps, about four hours at 20 tokens a second on a 24 GB card. The published 9.8 ran on Qwen3.8-27B in FP8 and BF16 through OpenRouter; a quantised copy is the same weights at lower precision. Readers in the HN thread (summary on zeli.app) report Q5 and above holding up where Q3 does not. Each step keeps its files; a stopped run resumes where it stopped.

Nothing leaves the machine: the runtime answers on localhost, state is under ~/.memdoor.

## Five small models against a frontier model: the team-solve result — Memdoor docs
URL: https://memdoor.ai/docs/team-solve
Description: Five Qwen3.8-27B agents as a Memdoor workflow: a mean of 9.8 of 10 on the first ten problems of GVS5H's LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes.

Home
Five small models against a frontier model: the team-solve result

Five Qwen3.8-27B agents as a Memdoor workflow: a mean of 9.8 of 10 on the first ten problems of GVS5H's LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes. The authors' harness: 9.6. Fable 5, one call: 8.0. All 50 runs published with every request and reply. Thread: Hacker News, 2026-10-31.

pass	Memdoor workflow	authors' harness	Fable 5, one call
1	10 / 10	9	7
2	10 / 10	10	8
3	10 / 10	10	10
4	10 / 10	9	8
5	9 / 10	10	7
mean	9.8	9.6	8.0
What was measured

GVS5H (Lee, 2026): a planner, two ideators, a solver, a manager and a repair worker, each from a fresh context, talking only through files on disk; a script that runs the samples decides success. The paper's claim: five copies of an open 27B organised this way match Fable 5 on hard competitive-programming problems.

The rebuild: eight YAML files, no code, no model named. Prompts, temperatures, the 128K reply cap, the ten-round loop and the cut-off handling are the authors', checked byte for byte against their code with a scripted model. Model: the same Qwen3.8-27B through OpenRouter. Problems: the first ten of their list, five passes each, graded on every hidden test with their corrected grader. The authors' columns: the regraded result files in their repository.

Cost: a median of 40 minutes and $0.39 a run; $35.79 for the 50.

What it does and does not show
Sample: ten problems, five passes, against the authors' 100. 9.8 and 9.6 are within noise. The result is parity with their harness.
Contamination: the contests date from spring 2025; the model may have seen them. Not ruled out for any column.
Fable 5: one call per problem, from the authors' files, no harness.
On these ten, the authors' own five-pass data: Fable 5 at 80, their harness at 96. The workflow's 98 reproduces that gap. Across their full 100: 92.4 and 90.4 (their patched_verdicts.json).
The loop sees the public samples; the score is the hidden tests.
Host: OpenRouter, not a local machine.
The lost problem: the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong answer and the team rewrote a correct program. Twice elsewhere a correct program was overwritten by a later round and recovered before the end. Both are gaps in the authors' loop, kept as is.

Runs, with each call's tokens, cost and host: bench/results/parity-5pass. Parity check, hosts, what the rebuild took, where it lost: NOTES.md.

Run it on your own problem
curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash
memdoor connect openrouter          # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt
memdoor connect local               # or no key: a model on this machine (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio)
mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem
memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait   # built in; an empty folder gets the sample problem; exit 0 when every sample passes

The built-in takes any task a prompt defines: /w team-solve <the task> in the window, or memdoor workflow run team-solve "<the task>" in the project. The output is what the task asks for: changes across a repository, a program, a document. A fresh judge checks what no command can. It ships in the binary, seeded into ~/.memdoor/workflows at the gateway's first boot; --model <id> puts every step on one model. Its prompts are not the authors', so the 9.8 above is not the built-in's: it has no benchmark score yet. The published runs used the steps in examples/workflows/team-solve, kept as they were. Your problem without a prompt: task.md and paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out in the folder. Program: solution.py, stdin in, compared to the samples with diff. The steps name no model; the /model pin answers, a local one included.

No key: memdoor connect local reaches Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM or LM Studio on this machine (how; the whole path). Ollama's default window is 4,096 tokens, too short for the coder's prompt: set 32K first, as that page shows. A hard problem: about 300K output tokens a run. Floor: a 27B at Q5 or above on a 24 GB card.

How it works
plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify
       └── ideate-b ──┘

Every agent prompt: "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat"; the paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. test and verify are command steps that run the samples; verify alone decides the run. One YAML file per step; requires: is the DAG; a role is its prompt. The files: examples/workflows/team-solve.

GVS5H (Gorilla vs. 5 Humans): Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
Results

Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend.

Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.

— the paper

Running the code

Needs uv and an API key for the model you want to test.

cd codebase/v2-current
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...

LCB_RELEASE=release_v6 \
ESCALATION_CLOUD_MAX_TOKENS=128000 \
ESCALATION_CLOUD_TIMEOUT=7200 \
MULTIAGENT_MODEL=openai:gpt-5.6-terra \
uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with 'datasets<4' --with numpy --with anthropic \
  python escalation/run_bench.py --engine multiagent --only lcb --lcb 100 --parallel 8
--engine multiagent runs the manager; --engine single is the one-call baseline.
Other models: anthropic:<model>, dashscope:<model>, openrouter:<model>, each with its own *_API_KEY.
The pass@1 score prints at the end. Results are written to runs/results.json, workspaces to runs/ws/.

## Headless, then attached — Memdoor docs
URL: https://memdoor.ai/docs/headless
Description: Every run is a conversation on your gateway, window or not: a turn from the window, the phone or the editor, a schedule, a workflow from a shell or CI, a…

Home
Headless, then attached

Every run is a conversation on your gateway, window or not: a turn from the window, the phone or the editor, a schedule, a workflow from a shell or CI, a spawned child. memdoor resume opens any of them. A run is left alone and rejoined live, not killed and started over.

The rule

Every command is headless except memdoor tui, the window. memdoor resume opens the window at a terminal and prints text into a pipe. No flag decides it. memdoor run, workflow run, cron add, guards and the rest take a prompt or arguments, write text or events and return an exit code. Stdin is the input when it is a pipe or a file. A terminal is never read.

The gateway: a background process on the machine the run belongs to, laptop or CI runner. memdoor run, workflow run, workflow resume, cron add, resume, tui and acp start one when none is running and set the machine up the first time. A run that must survive a closed laptop belongs on a box that stays on: memdoor gateway install there; laptop, ssh and phone are doors onto it.

Runs that need no window
Scheduled check. Inside a turn: cron(every: "20s", task: "is CI green?", times: 6), and the turn ends. From the shell: memdoor cron add --id nightly --schedule "0 6 * * *" --agent coder --message "…"; --workflow <name> schedules a workflow. Scheduled checks.
Workflow from the shell or CI. memdoor workflow run <name> starts the project's workflow and prints the run. memdoor workflow status <run-id>: each task's state. history <name>: earlier runs. On a CI runner: the installer, the key in the environment, the command with --wait; it starts the gateway, sets the runner up and exits with the run's outcome. On GitHub: one step, uses: guregodevo/memdoor-action@v1, the workflow's name and your key. Built in, no file in the repo: pr-triage, pr-review, security-review, write-tests, pr-description, explain-failure, issue-triage, fix-tests, release-notes, team-solve, team-backlog. Workflows.
Editor session. The coder in VS Code, Zed or JetBrains is a conversation on the same gateway. In your editor.
Phone, from a script. memdoor remote <id> prints the link /remote would, on stdout, and returns. The gateway holds the link for as long as it runs. Remote control.

Each answers into a conversation. A check's answer wakes the conversation that asked, and the agent acts on it.

A turn from a script

memdoor run: one coder turn, no window. Prompt from the arguments or stdin, answer on stdout, everything else on stderr, exit code the turn's receipt.

memdoor run "make the retry wait configurable and add a test"
git diff | memdoor run "review this diff; one line per finding"
memdoor run --json "fix the failing test" | jq -r 'select(.event=="done") | .receipt'

Arguments and a pipe together: the pipe is the input the prompt is about. --json streams NDJSON events (text, tool_start, tool_done, question, done); done carries the conversation id, the receipt and the exit code.

Exit	Meaning
0	the turn ended and what it changed was checked, or nothing needed a check
1	the gateway, the provider or the turn failed
2	it ended unverified: a change with no check after it, or a failing check
3	in a pipe, the agent asked a question nobody could answer and took the default; --yes answers the first option instead. At a terminal you answer it there.
130	ctrl-c or a TERM signal ended it; the conversation keeps what ran, memdoor resume <id> continues it

A turn from a script: the answer on stdout, the exit code, then the same run opened in a window

Each run is a conversation. Its id is on stderr at the end; memdoor resume <id> opens it in a window. --conversation <id> continues one.

memdoor workflow run <name> --wait: the same contract for a workflow. Progress on stderr, the files the run produced on stdout, exit 0 done, 2 failed, 1 stopped. A gate is reported and waited on. --stop-at-gate: exit 3 at a gate, the gate's review on stderr, for a job with nobody to approve; the run stays waiting on the gateway.

A walk through the doors

Run in this order on 11 October 2026, against a gateway that was not running when the first command started, in a scratch Go project whose Add returned a - b. The exit codes are the receipts.

Command	Exit	What it did
echo calc.go | memdoor run "which function does the file on stdin export? change nothing"	0	started the gateway, read stdin as the input, answered on stdout
memdoor run --json "run go test ./... and report; change nothing"	2	15 events; done carried ⚠ nothing changed · ran: go test FAIL
memdoor workflow run check --wait (test still broken)	2	stderr failed · 1/2 done, the failing task named
memdoor run "fix Add in calc.go so TestAdd passes, then run go test ./..."	0	✓ checked: 1 file changed · go build PASS · go test PASS
memdoor workflow run check --wait (green)	0	stderr done · 2/2 done

memdoor resume --last | head -6	0	your line with >, the answer, the receipt
memdoor --gateway 127.0.0.1:18799 providers	0	a bare host:port reaches the gateway

In CI

GitHub: one step, uses: guregodevo/memdoor-action@v1, a workflow (one of the nine built in, or yours), your key or a model inside the runner. The run's outcome is the job's. In CI. Elsewhere, three shell lines:

curl -fsSL "https://memdoor.ai/install.sh?ci=1" | MEMDOOR_CI=1 bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
memdoor workflow run pr-review --wait --stop-at-gate

To finish a CI run from a phone: the job starts its gateway (memdoor gateway &, memdoor gateway status until it answers, then memdoor run), prints the link with memdoor remote --last and waits on the gateway. The link and its QR code are in the job's log; the job stays up until you are done or its timeout ends it. The full step: Remote control. A runner's address is not reachable from a phone, so this step needs a gateway the phone can reach: a box, not a runner.

Coming back in
$ memdoor resume --all
Recent conversations:

      ID        TITLE                                        STARTED        LAST USED
   1. 41af4ac5  nightly: build the rule, grade it, file it   Oct 10 06:00   9m ago   ~/Dev/qant
   2. c0921b32  release                                      Oct 10 21:42   2h ago   ~/Dev/memdoor
   3. f9697a1e  make the wait ceiling configurable           Oct 10 19:01   5h ago   ~/Dev/throttle
$ memdoor resume 2

Into a pipe, the same command prints the conversation as text. No flag decides it:

memdoor resume 41af4ac5 | head -40
memdoor resume --last --follow     # text, and keep printing what the running turn does

Your lines start with >; the agent's are plain; a tool call is one ⏺ line. --gateway takes a bare host or IP as well as a URL: memdoor --gateway 192.168.1.10 resume --all | head.

The window opens on the conversation with its saved messages in view and the same session underneath. The next line is the next turn of that run. A turn running when you attach is shown from that moment, tool frames and answer; Esc interrupts it. Earlier work is in the saved messages, not replayed as frames. memdoor resume <id> takes the id a run printed, from any directory. Without --all the list is this folder's conversations.

A run waiting on you

A workflow gate shows ⏸ with the diff. Approve from the window (a) or from anywhere:

memdoor workflow approve <run-id> <task>
memdoor workflow changes <run-id> <task> "the notes miss the migration"

changes reruns the task with the comment and waits again. memdoor workflow resume <run-id> resumes a failed run at the failed step; finished tasks are skipped.

From your phone

/remote in a window: a link that is the terminal, end to end encrypted, so a run can be watched and answered from a phone. Remote control.

Letting a turn run

A turn judged unfinished by its receipts continues until it is shown done or a token budget is spent. The budget bounds an unattended turn. The harness.

If the gateway restarts

Conversations and runs are on disk. A window reconnects. A turn that was mid-run may have finished meanwhile; its result is in the saved messages, not replayed. memdoor workflow resume <run-id> continues a cut-off workflow run from its last finished task.
